title: The universal gate (Kern ch. 24)
hookLine: Avalokiteshvara hears every cry and comes in whatever form is needed

cards: A cry for help doesn't have to be loud. A text at two in the morning that only says: you up? A long pause on a phone call.

A friend who says I'm fine a little too quickly. Chapter twenty-four, in Kern's numbering, is about a bodhisattva whose whole work is hearing cries like that. You met him in year one, in the Heart Sutra.
Here the bodhisattva Akshayamati rises, bares one shoulder in respect, and asks the Buddha: why is this one called Avalokiteshvara?

teach.b: First, the answer. If beings in any kind of suffering hear this bodhisattva's name and call on it, the Buddha says, Avalokiteshvara hears them, and they are freed.
Second, the dangers, one by one, like a list of nights nobody wants to have.
Someone thrown into a great fire, and the fire does not burn. Someone swept along by a river, who finds shallow ground. Sailors blown toward an island of fierce spirits.
A prisoner under the executioner's sword, and the sword breaks. Chains that loosen. A caravan on a road full of bandits, where the leader tells everyone to call the name together.
The chapter turns inward too: those burning with desire, anger or confusion are freed by keeping this bodhisattva in mind. Third, the forms.

Like yesterday's visitor, Avalokiteshvara comes in whatever shape a person can be helped by: as a Buddha, as Brahma, as a merchant, a monk, a child. Kern's English calls the chapter the all-sided one.

teach.h: A GATE OPEN ON EVERY SIDE.
teach.b: The Chinese title, rendered in English as the universal gate, pictures it another way: a gate open on every side.
Fourth, the necklace. Akshayamati takes off a necklace of pearls worth a great deal and offers it. Avalokiteshvara won't take it, until the Buddha asks him to accept, out of kindness to the giver.
Then he divides it in two, and gives one half to Shakyamuni and the other to the stupa of the ancient Buddha Prabhutaratna.
The one who hears keeps nothing for himself.

how: Avalokiteshvara is honored across Mahayana and Vajrayana Buddhism; people call on the bodhisattva's name in danger and distress, and this chapter of the Lotus Sutra is recited as a teaching on compassion that hears.

o: a temple door that opens only on holy days
a path to heaven open to all who pray
the chapter of the bodhisattva who hears every cry

games.q: the universal gate: tap the pairs.

s: in the chapter, Avalokiteshvara keeps the necklace Akshayamati offers
he divides it in two, giving one half to Shakyamuni and one to Prabhutaratna's stupa.
the chapter says Avalokiteshvara appears in whatever form a person can be helped by
as a Buddha, as Brahma, as a merchant, a monk, a child.
the chapter speaks only of outer dangers like fire and floods
it also speaks of freedom from desire, anger and confusion.

games.q: you are Avalokiteshvara. Akshayamati offers you a precious necklace. you refuse, and the Buddha asks you to accept it. what do you do?
o: accept it, divide it in two and give both halves away
games.why: he accepts out of kindness to the giver, then gives one half to Shakyamuni and the other to Prabhutaratna's stupa.

practice: Let a recent hard moment surface, a small one is enough, and let it be there without fixing it.
If you're a Buddhist who calls on Avalokiteshvara, say the name softly now; if not, simply breathe as if someone were listening fully to that moment, with no hurry and no judgment.
Stay with it, breath by breath, and let the listening be wide.

wordCard.voice: The universal gate. The Lotus Sutra's chapter on Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva who hears every cry and comes in whatever form is needed. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the name of the bodhisattva of compassion, the one who hears in this chapter.

carryVoice: Your line: the one who hears. If a cry is about danger or self-harm, call or text 988 in the US, or local emergency help, any hour. I'll be here tomorrow.

sources.ref: Saddharmapundarika, ch. 24 (Kern numbering; ch. 25 in Kumarajiva's Chinese)
